title: One dark night (John, Dark Night, stanza 1)
hookLine: on a dark night, kindled with love, I went out unseen
tomorrow: what's the first thing you'd ask someone who vanished?

cards: Late at night, phone left on the counter, a door eased shut so nobody wakes. A scene like that usually spells trouble.
In a poem by John of the Cross, another Carmelite, someone slips out of a house at night, and the reason is love. The household is finally asleep. Nobody sees the door open.
And the one leaving isn't running from anything; she's going out to meet the one she loves, and she's happy.

teach.b: In John's Spanish it begins: "En una noche oscura, con ansias en amores inflamada."

In plain English the stanza goes something like this: on a dark night, kindled in love with longings, oh, happy chance, I went out unseen, my house being now at rest. Today dark night can mean a bleak stretch of life.
But look at what the night does in the poem. It isn't the enemy. It's cover, what lets the lover leave without being stopped.
And right in the dark comes a cry of joy: oh, happy chance.

teach.h: THE SOUL GOING OUT TO GOD.
teach.b: In his own commentary on the poem, John reads the one going out as the soul going toward God, and the quiet house as a self whose restless wants have finally gone still.

teach.h: THE NIGHT SHINETH AS THE DAY.
teach.b: A psalm has the same surprising night: "the darkness hideth not from thee; but the night shineth as the day."
Look back over the week and the same turn keeps coming: a peace given in trouble, hope beside a grave, a friend in the quiet, a God who stays while everything passes.
Now a night that is cover for love.

how: Carmelites and other Christians read John of the Cross's poems slowly, often alongside his own commentaries on them, as part of their prayer.

o: a night when God leaves you on your own
a long season of sadness and depression
a night that hides a soul going out in love

the popular sense. in the poem the night is cover for a lover slipping out, kindled in love.
John wrote his own commentary on the poem

the poem's first stanza is full of fear

games.q: your friend has been in a long, quiet stretch: no big feelings in prayer, nothing to report. she calls it her dark night and figures God's gone. what does John's first stanza offer?
o: the dark can be cover, where love slips out the door.
proof that something has gone badly wrong.
a sign to stop praying until the feelings return.
games.why: in the stanza the night is the lover's cover, and right in the middle comes oh, happy chance. here the dark isn't where God goes missing.

practice: If you can, step outside into the evening, or stand at a window as the light fades. Listen for one sound of the night coming on, a bird, a car, the wind, and stay with that one sound.
If you pray, let this be a small going-out toward God, unhurried and unseen.
